opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What I find most exciting is how hard robotics turns out to be in ways that surprise people. Things that are trivial for a toddler, like picking up a sock, folding a shirt, or wiping a table, are really hard for robots. That gap tells us something deep about intelligence. A lot of what we think of as "easy" is the result of a huge amount of physical experience and common sense about how the world works, and we don't know how to give machines that yet.

For me that's both a scientific question and a practical one. Scientifically, how do you build a system that can learn from experience, generalize to new situations, and adapt when something unexpected happens? Language models have shown what happens when you train on internet-scale data, but there's no internet of robot data. You have to think about where the data comes from, how to collect it, and how to use it efficiently. That makes it a really interesting research problem, because you can't just scale up one recipe.

Then there's the embodiment. When a robot acts in the world, it gets immediate, unforgiving feedback. Either the shirt got folded or it didn't. There's something very satisfying about that, and it keeps you honest about whether your ideas actually work.

And the potential impact is huge. If we can get robots that are general-purpose, that can handle the messiness and diversity of the real world, they could help with a huge range of tasks, in homes, in elder care, in manufacturing, in places where there's a lot of physical labor that people don't necessarily want to do. So it combines some of the deepest open questions in AI with the possibility of really changing how physical work gets done. That combination is what keeps me excited about it.

r001.rationale: The response connects robotics’ practical impact on physical work with the challenge of building machines that learn from physical experience, generalize, and adapt to the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what gets me most excited about robotics is that it's one of the few places where you can't fake your way around the hard problems of intelligence. If you build a language model and it says something a little off, the text is still there and it kind of reads fine. If a robot is a little off, it drops the cup or knocks over the plant. The physical world grades you, and it grades you honestly.

So robotics forces you to confront what it actually means to understand something. A model can talk about pouring coffee all day, but can it pour coffee? Can it do it in a kitchen it's never seen, with a mug that's a different shape, when the lighting is weird? That gap between knowing about the world and being able to act in it is, to me, the most interesting open question in AI right now.

The other thing I love is that it's fundamentally a data problem, but a strange one. With language, the internet gave us this enormous free dataset of humans being smart. There's no equivalent for robots. Nobody has been uploading trillions of examples of motor torques and gripper positions. So we have to think really carefully about where experience comes from: teleoperation, simulation, video of people, robots learning from their own mistakes. Figuring out how to get the right data at the right scale, and how to make models that generalize from far less of it than you'd like, feels like a puzzle that's genuinely unsolved rather than one where we just need to turn the crank.

And honestly, part of it is that it's just fun. When a policy finally works and you watch a robot fold a shirt it's never seen before, there's this moment where you feel like you learned something true about learning itself. That keeps me going.

r001.rationale: The response clearly connects robotics’ physical-world consequences with the challenge of machine intelligence, but it does not clearly present perception as part of that challenge.

astra-6.text:
What I find exciting is that robotics forces us to confront what it really means for a system to learn and act in the world. A robot doesn’t just need to recognize what’s in an image. It needs to decide what to do, take an action, and deal with the consequences—and those consequences change what it sees next.

There’s also this fascinating gap between what people find easy and what machines find easy. Picking up an unfamiliar object or opening a door feels almost effortless to us, but it requires a lot of intelligence: understanding the environment, adapting to uncertainty, and recovering when something doesn’t work.

That makes robotics a really compelling setting for studying learning. How can a system use its past experience to handle something new? How can it learn from a small amount of interaction? Those are fundamental questions about intelligence, and with robots you get to test the answers in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response connects perception, learning, and intelligence in machines with acting and testing ideas in the physical world, capturing robotics as a meeting point with real-world action.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find really exciting is that robotics forces us to confront what it means for a machine to learn and make decisions in the real world. You don’t just need to recognize what’s in an image. You need to figure out what to do, take an action, and deal with how that action changes what you see next.

And there’s this interesting tension: humans can pick up a new object or learn a new task with very little experience, while robots still need a lot of data and often struggle when something changes. How do we build systems that can draw on their previous experience, adapt to a new situation, and keep learning? That brings together some really fundamental questions about intelligence with a very concrete test: can the robot actually do the task?

r001.rationale: The response connects machine perception and learning to making decisions and acting in the real world, with the robot’s ability to do the task as a concrete test.
